lines.01-man-s-search-for-meaning: A psychiatrist's account of surviving the Nazi camps, and his case that a reason to live makes suffering bearable.
lines.02-the-three-body-problem: During China's Cultural Revolution, a young astrophysicist joins a secret military project whose consequences surface decades later.
lines.03-hooked: How companies build products people use out of habit, through a loop of trigger, action, variable reward and investment.
lines.04-true-names: A hacker in a shared virtual world is unmasked by the government and forced to hunt a more dangerous one.
lines.05-liftoff: How SpaceX's small early team failed three times on a remote Pacific island before reaching orbit in 2008.
lines.06-flow: People are happiest when fully absorbed in a challenge matching their skills, a state called flow that anyone can cultivate.
lines.07-the-founders: The chaotic early years of PayPal, whose founders, including Thiel, Musk and Levchin, went on to shape Silicon Valley.
lines.08-nuclear-war: A fact-based, minute-by-minute scenario of how a surprise North Korean attack could escalate to global nuclear war within 72 minutes.
lines.09-siddhartha: In ancient India, in the Buddha's time, a young Brahmin leaves his family to seek spiritual enlightenment.
lines.10-the-thinking-machine: How Jensen Huang built Nvidia from a 1993 graphics-chip startup into the company whose chips power modern AI.
lines.11-zero-to-one: Real progress comes from creating something new, not copying what works, and great startups escape competition by building monopolies.
lines.12-consider-phlebas: In a galactic war, a shape-shifter working against the Culture is sent to capture a fugitive Culture AI.
lines.13-atomic-habits: Small habits compound like interest, and you change behavior by making good habits obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying.
lines.14-the-dream-machine: How J.C.R. Licklider, a psychologist funding computer research at ARPA, set personal computing and the internet in motion.
lines.15-when-breath-becomes-air: A neurosurgeon in training, diagnosed with terminal lung cancer at 36, reflects on what makes life worth living.
lines.16-superintelligence: Machines smarter than us could slip beyond human control, so the problem of controlling them must be solved first.
lines.17-elon-musk: Musk's life from a South African childhood through Zip2 and PayPal to his near-ruinous bets on Tesla and SpaceX.
lines.18-foundation: A mathematician foresees the Galactic Empire's fall and plots to cut the coming dark age from 30,000 years to 1,000.
lines.19-don-t-make-me-think: Websites and apps should be self-evident, because users scan rather than read, and cheap usability tests reveal where they stumble.
lines.20-the-precipice: A philosopher estimates a one-in-six chance of existential catastrophe this century, mainly from human-made risks like AI and engineered pandemics.
lines.21-becoming-steve-jobs: How Steve Jobs, ousted from Apple in 1985, matured at NeXT and Pixar into the leader who rebuilt Apple.
lines.22-a-deepness-in-the-sky: Rival fleets of human traders and tyrants reach a world of spider-like aliens whose sun switches off for centuries.
lines.23-the-mom-test: Even your mom will lie about liking your idea, so ask customers about their lives and past behavior instead.
lines.24-the-dark-forest: The second Three-Body book: four people are given unchecked power to plan humanity's defense, each keeping the plan inside their own head.
lines.25-excellent-advice-for-living: About 450 tweet-length bits of advice on work, money, relationships and creativity, first written for Kelly's grown children.
lines.26-permutation-city: In a future where minds can be uploaded into computers, a man runs unsettling experiments on his own digital copy.
lines.27-the-hard-thing-about-hard-things: Blunt advice on a CEO's hardest calls, like layoffs and demoting friends, drawn from steering Loudcloud and Opsware through near-collapse.
lines.28-human-compatible: An AI pioneer argues that giving machines fixed objectives is dangerous, and that they should instead learn what humans want.
lines.29-reentry: How SpaceX built Falcon 9 and Dragon, learned to land and reuse rockets, and began flying NASA astronauts.
lines.30-bhagavad-gita: On a battlefield, Krishna counsels the reluctant warrior Arjuna on duty and self-mastery, in a translation with explanatory introductions.
lines.31-the-player-of-games: A bored champion game-player from the utopian Culture is sent to a cruel empire where one game decides who rules.
lines.32-how-the-internet-happened: A history of the web's commercial era, from the Netscape browser through the dot-com bubble to the iPhone.
lines.33-outliers: Exceptional success comes less from individual talent than from opportunity, timing, cultural background and about 10,000 hours of practice.
lines.34-the-maniac: A novel built around John von Neumann, following his ideas from the atomic bomb to computers to AlphaGo.
lines.35-founders-at-work: Interviews with founders of Apple, PayPal, Hotmail and other tech companies about what happened in their earliest days.
lines.36-life-3-0: An MIT physicist surveys how advanced AI could reshape work, war and life itself, and which futures to steer toward.
lines.37-benjamin-franklin: Benjamin Franklin's rise from runaway printer's apprentice to scientist and diplomat, and how his practical spirit shaped America's character.
lines.38-use-of-weapons: The Culture tries to re-enlist Zakalwe, its veteran agent in other worlds' wars, while alternate chapters rewind his past.
lines.39-the-alignment-problem: How AI systems learn the wrong lessons, from biased predictions to gamed rewards, and the researchers trying to fix it.
lines.40-profiles-of-the-future: Essays on the limits of the possible, and why predictions about technology fail from lack of nerve or imagination.
lines.41-elon-musk: Built on two years shadowing Musk, a biography running from his harsh South African childhood to buying Twitter.
lines.42-why-greatness-cannot-be-planned: Ambitious achievements come from following what's interesting, not from chasing a fixed objective.
lines.43-death-s-end: The Three-Body trilogy's finale follows an aerospace engineer who wakes centuries later, holding choices that will shape humanity's future.
lines.44-persuasive-technology: A Stanford researcher shows how websites, software and mobile devices can be designed to change what people think and do.
lines.45-the-man-who-remade-india: A biography of P. V. Narasimha Rao, the unlikely prime minister who opened India's economy after the 1991 crisis.
lines.46-there-is-no-antimemetics-division: A secret division fights antimemes, things that erase themselves from memory, in a war almost nobody can remember.
lines.47-peak: Expertise is built, not inborn, through deliberate practice: focused, feedback-driven work just beyond one's current ability.
lines.48-this-is-water: A 2005 commencement speech arguing that real education means learning to choose what you pay attention to, every day.
lines.49-the-innovator-s-dilemma: Why well-run leading companies, by listening to their best customers, lose out to cheaper, simpler disruptive technologies.
lines.50-boom-bubbles-and-the-end-of-stagnatio: Speculative bubbles can be good: the same manias drove the Manhattan Project and Apollo, and could end today's stagnation.
lines.51-what-do-you-care-what-other-people-th: Feynman's stories of his father, his first wife Arline, and his investigation into the 1986 Challenger shuttle disaster.
lines.52-shoe-dog: Nike's co-founder recounts building the company, from selling Japanese running shoes out of his car to its 1980 IPO.
lines.53-the-selfish-gene: Evolution is best seen from the gene's point of view, with organisms as survival machines, which explains even altruism.
lines.54-poor-charlie-s-almanack: Eleven talks by Warren Buffett's longtime partner on investing, human misjudgment, and thinking with mental models from many fields.
